title: Red Blood Cell
sections: Erythrocyte Membrane, Gas Transport & Blood Groups (Q21-Q40)

questions.text: Within the cellular composition of human whole blood, red blood cells (erythrocytes) constitute approximately what proportion of all formed elements?
questions.explanation: Red blood cells vastly outnumber white blood cells and platelets, making up approximately $99%$ of all formed (cellular) elements in human blood.

questions.text: Red blood cells play a central role in carbon dioxide ($CO_2$) transport. Approximately what proportion of blood $CO_2$ is transported as bicarbonate ions ($HCO_3^-$), and which RBC enzyme catalyzes this reaction?
options: $63%$ to $70%$; catalyzed by carbonic anhydrase
$97%$; catalyzed by catalase
$20%$; catalyzed by ferrochelatase
$7%$; catalyzed by myeloperoxidase
questions.correctAnswer: A. $63%$ to $70%$; catalyzed by carbonic anhydrase
questions.explanation: Roughly $63%$ to $70%$ of $CO_2$ is carried as bicarbonate formed rapidly inside RBCs by carbonic anhydrase, while $20%$ to $23%$ is carried as carbaminohaemoglobin and $7%$ dissolved in plasma.

questions.text: What is the immunological mechanism underlying haemolytic disease of the newborn (erythroblastosis fetalis) due to Rh incompatibility?
options: Maternal IgM anti-A antibodies cross the placenta during the first trimester
Fetal IgG antibodies cross the placenta to destroy maternal RBCs
An Rh-negative mother sensitized by Rh-positive fetal RBCs produces IgG anti-D antibodies that cross the placenta in subsequent Rh-positive pregnancies and lyse fetal RBCs
Maternal complement proteins directly dissolve fetal bone marrow stem cells
questions.correctAnswer: C. An Rh-negative mother sensitized by Rh-positive fetal RBCs produces IgG anti-D antibodies that cross the placenta in subsequent Rh-positive pregnancies and lyse fetal RBCs
questions.explanation: During delivery of a first Rh-positive baby, fetal RBCs sensitize an Rh-negative mother to form IgG anti-D antibodies, which cross the placenta in subsequent pregnancies and cause fetal haemolysis.

questions.text: What outer membrane component imparts a net negative surface charge (zeta potential) to red blood cells, helping prevent spontaneous clumping in the circulation?
options: Free cholesterol molecules
Intracellular spectrin dimers
Sialic acid residues on membrane glycophorins
Phosphatidylserine on the inner leaflet
questions.correctAnswer: C. Sialic acid residues on membrane glycophorins
questions.explanation: Sialic acid (N-acetylneuraminic acid) residues attached to transmembrane glycoproteins such as glycophorins create a negative surface charge that generates mutual electrostatic repulsion between RBCs.

questions.text: Which physiological phenomenon describes the rightward shift of the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve caused by elevated $pCO_2$ and decreased pH in active tissues, and which other factors also shift the curve to the right?
options: Haldane effect; decreased temperature and decreased $2,3$-DPG
Hamburger phenomenon; increased pH and decreased $2,3$-DPG
Donnan effect; decreased temperature and fetal haemoglobin
Bohr effect; increased temperature and increased $2,3$-DPG
questions.correctAnswer: D. Bohr effect; increased temperature and increased $2,3$-DPG
questions.explanation: The Bohr effect describes reduced $O_2$ affinity at high $pCO_2$ and low pH, promoting oxygen unloading in tissues; increased temperature and elevated $2,3$-DPG also shift the curve to the right.

questions.text: Which physiological states are normally associated with a slight physiological DECREASE in the circulating red blood cell count?
options: High altitude and vigorous exercise
Deep sleep, high barometric pressure, and normal pregnancy (due to plasma volume expansion/haemodilution)
Newborn infancy and emotional stress
Exposure to high environmental temperature
questions.correctAnswer: B. Deep sleep, high barometric pressure, and normal pregnancy (due to plasma volume expansion/haemodilution)
questions.explanation: During sleep, reduced metabolic demand lowers the RBC count slightly; at high barometric pressure, increased $O_2$ tension suppresses erythropoiesis; and in pregnancy, increased plasma volume causes physiological haemodilution.

questions.text: Why is the intermediate normoblast also termed the polychromatic erythroblast?
options: It contains multiple fragmented nuclei
It lacks all cytoplasmic RNA and ribosomes
It stains exclusively with basic methylene blue dye
It contains both basophilic RNA and newly visible acidophilic haemoglobin, taking up both acidic and basic stains
questions.correctAnswer: D. It contains both basophilic RNA and newly visible acidophilic haemoglobin, taking up both acidic and basic stains
questions.explanation: Because haemoglobin first becomes visible in the intermediate normoblast ($10$ to $12\ \mu\text{m}$) while basophilic RNA is still present, the cytoplasm exhibits polychromatic staining.

questions.text: Haemolysis is defined as the rupture of the erythrocyte membrane with release of haemoglobin. Which organ serves as the primary physiological site of senile RBC destruction and is termed the "graveyard of red blood cells"?
options: Kidney
Thymus
Pancreas
Spleen (along with the liver and bone marrow)
questions.correctAnswer: D. Spleen (along with the liver and bone marrow)
questions.explanation: Senile erythrocytes are primarily destroyed by macrophages of the reticuloendothelial system in the spleen ("graveyard of RBCs"), as well as in the liver and bone marrow.

questions.text: What is the exact molecular genetic defect responsible for Sickle Cell Disease (Haemoglobin S)?
options: Complete deletion of all four $\alpha$-globin genes on chromosome $16$
A single point mutation in the $\beta$-globin gene substituting valine for glutamic acid at the $6\text{th}$ amino acid position
Substitution of lysine for glutamic acid at position $6$ of the $\alpha$-globin chain
Deficiency of the enzyme glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD)
questions.correctAnswer: B. A single point mutation in the $\beta$-globin gene substituting valine for glutamic acid at the $6\text{th}$ amino acid position
questions.explanation: Sickle cell disease results from a single nucleotide substitution in the $\beta$-globin gene, replacing hydrophilic glutamic acid with hydrophobic valine at position $6$ ($\beta^6\ \text{Glu}\rightarrow\text{Val}$), producing HbS.

questions.text: Which two endocrine hormones physiologically stimulate erythropoiesis by enhancing erythropoietin production or increasing general tissue oxygen demand?
options: Testosterone and thyroxine
Oestrogen and calcitonin
Melatonin and oxytocin
Parathyroid hormone and aldosterone
questions.correctAnswer: A. Testosterone and thyroxine
questions.explanation: Testosterone directly stimulates erythropoiesis and erythropoietin secretion (accounting for higher male RBC counts), while thyroxine increases general metabolic rate and oxygen consumption, indirectly stimulating erythropoiesis.

questions.text: Which statement accurately reflects Landsteiner's Law and explains why its second part does NOT apply to the Rh blood group system?
options: Part 1: if an antigen is present on RBCs, its antibody is absent in plasma; Part 2: if an antigen is absent, its antibody is present—this fails in the Rh system because Rh-negative individuals lack natural anti-D antibodies without prior sensitization
Part 1 states antigens and antibodies coexist; Part 2 fails in the Rh system because Rh antigens are in plasma
Both parts apply strictly to the Rh system but not to the ABO system
Part 2 fails in the Rh system because Rh-positive individuals naturally carry anti-D antibodies
questions.correctAnswer: A. Part 1: if an antigen is present on RBCs, its antibody is absent in plasma; Part 2: if an antigen is absent, its antibody is present—this fails in the Rh system because Rh-negative individuals lack natural anti-D antibodies without prior sensitization
questions.explanation: Landsteiner's Law governs the ABO system, where antibodies occur naturally against absent antigens. In the Rh system, anti-D antibodies are immune antibodies formed only after exposure to Rh-positive blood.

questions.text: What is the normal specific gravity of human red blood cells, which causes them to settle below the plasma layer during centrifugation?
questions.explanation: The specific gravity of RBCs ($1.092$ to $1.101$) is significantly higher than that of plasma ($1.022$ to $1.026$) and whole blood ($1.052$ to $1.061$).

questions.text: What is the polypeptide chain composition and approximate molecular weight of normal adult haemoglobin (HbA)?
options: Two $\alpha$-chains ($141$ amino acids each) and two $\beta$-chains ($146$ amino acids each); molecular weight $\approx 68,000$
Two $\alpha$-chains ($146$ amino acids each) and two $\beta$-chains ($141$ amino acids each); molecular weight $\approx 34,000$
Two $\alpha$-chains and two $\gamma$-chains; molecular weight $\approx 120,000$
Four identical $\beta$-chains; molecular weight $\approx 68,000$
questions.correctAnswer: A. Two $\alpha$-chains ($141$ amino acids each) and two $\beta$-chains ($146$ amino acids each); molecular weight $\approx 68,000$
questions.explanation: Normal adult haemoglobin (HbA, $\approx 97%$ of adult Hb) is a tetramer of two $\alpha$-chains ($141$ aa each) and two $\beta$-chains ($146$ aa each), with a molecular weight of about $68,000$.

questions.text: Why is Mean Corpuscular Haemoglobin Concentration (MCHC) regarded as the most reliable absolute index of cellular haemoglobin saturation?
options: It relies solely on the white blood cell count
Its calculation does not depend on the RBC count, which is prone to greater manual counting error
It measures only fetal haemoglobin concentration
It remains unchanged even in severe hypochromic states
questions.correctAnswer: B. Its calculation does not depend on the RBC count, which is prone to greater manual counting error
questions.explanation: Because MCHC uses only haemoglobin concentration and packed cell volume (PCV), it avoids potential errors in RBC enumeration and directly reflects true intracellular haemoglobin concentration.

questions.text: Within the bone marrow haemopoietic lineage, which committed progenitor cell directly gives rise to the erythroid series?
options: Lymphoid stem cell (LSC)
Colony-forming unit-granulocyte/monocyte (CFU-GM)
Colony-forming unit-megakaryocyte (CFU-M)
Colony-forming unit-erythrocyte (CFU-E)
questions.correctAnswer: D. Colony-forming unit-erythrocyte (CFU-E)
questions.explanation: Pluripotent haemopoietic stem cells differentiate into committed myeloid progenitors, among which CFU-E is strictly committed to developing into erythrocytes.

questions.text: What is the normal average circulating lifespan of a mature human red blood cell?
options: $30$ days
$60$ days
$120$ days
$240$ days
questions.correctAnswer: C. $120$ days
questions.explanation: Mature human erythrocytes circulate in the bloodstream for an average lifespan of $120$ days before being removed by the reticuloendothelial system.

questions.text: Why does true "hyperchromia" (supersaturation of haemoglobin beyond normal MCHC) not physiologically occur in red blood cells?
options: Haemoglobin cannot bind iron above $20\ \text{pg}$ per cell

Intracellular haemoglobin is already near its physical solubility limit in normal RBCs; cells that appear darker (such as spherocytes) look darker due to increased thickness rather than true haemoglobin supersaturation
Acidic dyes cannot stain haemoglobin above $30%$ concentration
Red blood cells actively pump excess haemoglobin out into plasma
questions.correctAnswer: B. Intracellular haemoglobin is already near its physical solubility limit in normal RBCs; cells that appear darker (such as spherocytes) look darker due to increased thickness rather than true haemoglobin supersaturation
questions.explanation: Normal RBCs are already near maximal haemoglobin solubility ($\approx 34$ to $36\ \text{g/dL}$). Apparent "hyperchromia" in spherocytes is an optical effect of greater cell thickness and absence of central pallor.

questions.text: In healthy adults over $20$ years of age, fatty yellow marrow replaces red marrow in the shafts of long bones. Which sites continue active erythropoiesis throughout adulthood?
options: Membranous (flat) bones such as vertebrae, sternum, ribs, iliac bones, and skull, plus proximal epiphyses of long bones
Mid-shafts (diaphyses) of the femur, tibia, and humerus
Splenic white pulp and regional lymph nodes
Renal cortex and adrenal medulla
questions.correctAnswer: A. Membranous (flat) bones such as vertebrae, sternum, ribs, iliac bones, and skull, plus proximal epiphyses of long bones
questions.explanation: After age $20$, erythropoiesis is restricted to membranous bones (vertebrae, sternum, ribs, scapula, iliac bones, skull) and the proximal ends of long bones.

questions.text: How is the iron liberated from destroyed red blood cells conserved and recycled by the body?
options: Stored as ferritin/hemosiderin in macrophages and hepatocytes or transported bound to transferrin back to the bone marrow for new erythropoiesis
Excreted completely in the bile along with bilirubin
Eliminated rapidly via renal glomerular filtration
Converted into carbonic anhydrase within plasma
questions.correctAnswer: A. Stored as ferritin/hemosiderin in macrophages and hepatocytes or transported bound to transferrin back to the bone marrow for new erythropoiesis
questions.explanation: Iron is tightly conserved; liberated iron either combines with apoferritin to form ferritin (and hemosiderin) for storage or binds apotransferrin (forming transferrin) to return to red bone marrow.

questions.text: Derived from the Greek roots erythros (red) and kytos (cell), how is a mature human erythrocyte most accurately defined?
options: A nucleated, phagocytic cell specialized for immune defence
A cytoplasmic fragment derived from bone marrow megakaryocytes
A specialized, non-nucleated, haemoglobin-containing blood cell adapted for respiratory gas transport
A self-replicating stem cell circulating within the peripheral vasculature
questions.correctAnswer: C. A specialized, non-nucleated, haemoglobin-containing blood cell adapted for respiratory gas transport
questions.explanation: Mature human erythrocytes are specialized, non-nucleated, biconcave blood cells rich in haemoglobin, whose primary role is transporting respiratory gases.

questions.text: Which non-respiratory function of red blood cells is determined by the presence of specific agglutinogens on their plasma membrane?
options: Blood coagulation cascade initiation
Blood group determination
Antibody synthesis
Complement activation
questions.correctAnswer: B. Blood group determination
questions.explanation: Red blood cells carry genetically determined surface antigens (agglutinogens such as A, B, and Rh/D) on their plasma membrane, which determine an individual's blood group.
questions.section: Erythrocyte Membrane, Gas Transport & Blood Groups

questions.text: Cyanosis—the bluish discoloration of skin and mucous membranes—typically becomes clinically apparent when the concentration of deoxygenated haemoglobin in capillary blood exceeds which threshold?
options: $1\ \text{g/dL}$
$5\ \text{g/dL}$
$10\ \text{g/dL}$
$15\ \text{g/dL}$
questions.correctAnswer: B. $5\ \text{g/dL}$
questions.explanation: Cyanosis is determined by the absolute concentration of reduced (deoxygenated) haemoglobin rather than percentage saturation alone, appearing when capillary deoxyhaemoglobin exceeds $5\ \text{g/dL}$.
questions.section: Erythrocyte Membrane, Gas Transport & Blood Groups

questions.text: Which of the following is a primary physiological advantage of the biconcave discoid shape of a mature red blood cell?
options: High surface-area-to-volume ratio facilitating rapid gas diffusion and easy deformability through narrow capillaries
Increased membrane tension during minor osmotic volume changes
Enhanced capacity for mitotic division within the microcirculation
Greater resistance to oxygen binding in pulmonary capillaries
questions.correctAnswer: A. High surface-area-to-volume ratio facilitating rapid gas diffusion and easy deformability through narrow capillaries
questions.explanation: The biconcave contour maximizes the surface-area-to-volume ratio for rapid $O_2$ and $CO_2$ diffusion, allows erythrocytes to deform through capillaries narrower than their own diameter, and accommodates slight volume increases without rupturing.
questions.section: Erythrocyte Membrane, Gas Transport & Blood Groups

questions.text: Approximately $10%$ of glucose metabolized in erythrocytes is shunted through the hexose monophosphate (pentose phosphate) pathway. What is the primary protective role of this pathway?
options: Generating NADPH to keep glutathione in its reduced state (GSH), protecting haemoglobin and membrane lipids from oxidative damage
Synthesizing ribose sugars for continuous DNA replication
Producing excess ATP during muscular exercise
Synthesizing new globin polypeptide chains
questions.correctAnswer: A. Generating NADPH to keep glutathione in its reduced state (GSH), protecting haemoglobin and membrane lipids from oxidative damage
questions.explanation: Initiated by glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD), the hexose monophosphate shunt generates NADPH to maintain reduced glutathione (GSH), which neutralizes reactive oxygen species.
questions.section: Erythrocyte Membrane, Gas Transport & Blood Groups

questions.text: In peripheral blood smear morphology, what do the terms anisocytosis and poikilocytosis specifically denote respectively?
options: Variation in RBC colour; variation in RBC count
Variation in RBC size; variation in RBC shape
Presence of nucleated RBCs; presence of reticulocytes
Variation in RBC shape; variation in RBC size
questions.correctAnswer: B. Variation in RBC size; variation in RBC shape
questions.explanation: Anisocytosis refers to abnormal variation in erythrocyte size (e.g., coexistence of microcytes and macrocytes), whereas poikilocytosis refers to abnormal variation in erythrocyte shape.
questions.section: Erythrocyte Membrane, Gas Transport & Blood Groups

questions.text: During the initial mesoblastic stage of intrauterine erythropoiesis (first $2$ months of fetal life), where are red blood cells primarily produced?
options: Mesenchyme of the yolk sac
Hepatic sinusoids
Red bone marrow
Splenic red pulp
questions.correctAnswer: A. Mesenchyme of the yolk sac
questions.explanation: During the mesoblastic stage (first $2$ months of gestation), primitive erythrocytes are produced from the mesenchyme of the yolk sac.
questions.section: Erythrocyte Membrane, Gas Transport & Blood Groups

questions.text: In a standard osmotic fragility test using serial dilutions of sodium chloride, at what approximate saline concentrations do the onset and completion of normal RBC haemolysis occur?
options: Onset at $0.45%$ NaCl; completion at $0.35%$ NaCl
Onset at $0.90%$ NaCl; completion at $0.60%$ NaCl
Onset at $0.75%$ NaCl; completion at $0.50%$ NaCl
Onset at $0.20%$ NaCl; completion at $0.05%$ NaCl
questions.correctAnswer: A. Onset at $0.45%$ NaCl; completion at $0.35%$ NaCl
questions.explanation: Normal RBCs remain intact in isotonic ($0.9%$) saline down to $0.6%$ NaCl; osmotic haemolysis begins around $0.45%$ NaCl (lysing older cells) and is complete around $0.35%$ NaCl.
questions.section: Erythrocyte Membrane, Gas Transport & Blood Groups

questions.text: What is the underlying structural defect in Hereditary Spherocytosis, and how does it affect the osmotic fragility of affected red blood cells?
options: Deficiency of intrinsic factor; decreases osmotic fragility
Point mutation in the $\beta$-globin chain; leaves osmotic fragility completely unchanged

Genetic defect in erythrocyte membrane cytoskeletal proteins (such as spectrin, ankyrin, or Band 3), causing membrane loss, spherical RBCs, increased osmotic fragility, and premature splenic destruction
Deficiency of carbonic anhydrase; causes crenation in hypotonic saline
questions.correctAnswer: C. Genetic defect in erythrocyte membrane cytoskeletal proteins (such as spectrin, ankyrin, or Band 3), causing membrane loss, spherical RBCs, increased osmotic fragility, and premature splenic destruction
questions.explanation: Defects in cytoskeletal anchoring proteins (spectrin, ankyrin, Band 3, protein 4.2) cause progressive loss of membrane surface area, converting biconcave discs into rigid spherocytes with markedly increased osmotic fragility that are trapped and destroyed in the spleen.
questions.section: Erythrocyte Membrane, Gas Transport & Blood Groups

questions.text: Approximately what percentage of total oxygen in arterial blood is transported in chemical combination with haemoglobin inside red blood cells?
questions.explanation: About $97%$ of arterial oxygen is carried bound to haemoglobin as oxyhaemoglobin, while only about $3%$ is physically dissolved in plasma.
questions.section: Erythrocyte Membrane, Gas Transport & Blood Groups

questions.text: Among the six antigens of the Rh blood group system ($C, D, E, c, d, e$), which specific antigen is the most strongly immunogenic and determines whether an individual is Rh-positive?
options: C antigen
D antigen
E antigen
c antigen
questions.correctAnswer: B. D antigen
questions.explanation: The D antigen is far more antigenic than the other Rh antigens; its presence on the RBC membrane defines an individual as Rh-positive, while its absence defines Rh-negative status.
questions.section: Erythrocyte Membrane, Gas Transport & Blood Groups

questions.text: Whole blood is approximately five times more viscous than water. Which two components are the primary determinants of blood viscosity?
options: Platelets and dissolved electrolytes
White blood cells and chylomicrons
Dissolved gases and glucose
Red blood cells and plasma proteins
questions.correctAnswer: D. Red blood cells and plasma proteins
questions.explanation: Blood viscosity depends primarily on the concentration of red blood cells (haematocrit) and the concentration of plasma proteins.
questions.section: Erythrocyte Membrane, Gas Transport & Blood Groups

questions.text: Which molecular property of haemoglobin accounts for the characteristic sigmoid (S-shaped) contour of the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve?
options: Cooperative binding (positive allostery), where binding of the first $O_2$ shifts Hb from the T-state to the R-state and increases affinity at the remaining heme sites
Independent, identical oxygen affinity across all four heme sites
Competitive binding between oxygen and plasma albumin
Irreversible covalent attachment of the fourth oxygen molecule
questions.correctAnswer: A. Cooperative binding (positive allostery), where binding of the first $O_2$ shifts Hb from the T-state to the R-state and increases affinity at the remaining heme sites
questions.explanation: Cooperative binding among the four subunits transitions haemoglobin from the low-affinity tense (T) state to the high-affinity relaxed (R) state as successive $O_2$ molecules bind, creating the sigmoid curve.
questions.section: Erythrocyte Membrane, Gas Transport & Blood Groups

questions.text: Which group of normal physiological conditions is characteristically associated with a physiological INCREASE in the circulating red blood cell count?
options: Deep sleep, pregnancy, and high barometric pressure
Advanced old age, recumbent posture, and morning hours
Prolonged fasting and haemodilution
Newborn infancy ($6$ to $7\ \text{million}/\text{mm}^3$), high altitude, vigorous muscular exercise, and emotional excitement
questions.correctAnswer: D. Newborn infancy ($6$ to $7\ \text{million}/\text{mm}^3$), high altitude, vigorous muscular exercise, and emotional excitement
questions.explanation: RBC count physiologically rises in newborns (due to intrauterine hypoxia), at high altitudes (hypoxic EPO drive), and during exercise or emotional excitement (sympathetic splenic contraction and haemoconcentration).
questions.section: Erythrocyte Membrane, Gas Transport & Blood Groups

questions.text: Which microscopic feature specifically characterizes the early normoblast (basophilic erythroblast) stage of erythropoiesis?
options: Disappearance of nucleoli with chromatin condensation and deeply basophilic cytoplasm
Presence of an extruded pyknotic ink-spot nucleus
Polychromatic cytoplasm containing visible haemoglobin
Presence of a supravital reticular network without a nucleus
questions.correctAnswer: A. Disappearance of nucleoli with chromatin condensation and deeply basophilic cytoplasm
questions.explanation: The early normoblast ($15\ \mu\text{m}$) is marked by the disappearance of nucleoli, condensation of chromatin into a dense network, and strongly basophilic cytoplasm.
questions.section: Erythrocyte Membrane, Gas Transport & Blood Groups

questions.text: In adult red bone marrow, roughly $75%$ of haemopoiesis produces leukocytes while $25%$ produces erythrocytes, yet circulating RBCs outnumber WBCs by about $500:1$. What explains this ratio?
options: Erythrocytes have a vastly longer circulating lifespan ($120$ days) than most leukocytes ($\frac{1}{2}$ to $15$ days)
Erythrocytes undergo continuous binary fission in the peripheral blood
Leukocytes are destroyed immediately before leaving the bone marrow
Only $1%$ of newly formed leukocytes enter the bloodstream
questions.correctAnswer: A. Erythrocytes have a vastly longer circulating lifespan ($120$ days) than most leukocytes ($\frac{1}{2}$ to $15$ days)
questions.explanation: Because leukocytes have a much shorter lifespan than erythrocytes, the bone marrow must devote a greater proportion of its production capacity to leukocytes to maintain their circulating counts.
questions.section: Erythrocyte Membrane, Gas Transport & Blood Groups

questions.text: How does primary polycythaemia (polycythaemia vera) differ pathophysiologically from secondary polycythaemia?
options: Primary polycythaemia is caused by high-altitude hypoxia with high EPO; secondary is a bone marrow neoplasm with low EPO
Both primary and secondary polycythaemia are caused exclusively by dehydration

Primary polycythaemia is an autonomous myeloproliferative disorder of the bone marrow with suppressed (low) erythropoietin levels, whereas secondary polycythaemia is driven by chronic hypoxia or excess erythropoietin secretion
Primary polycythaemia affects only RBCs without affecting WBCs or platelets; secondary polycythaemia elevates only platelets
questions.correctAnswer: C. Primary polycythaemia is an autonomous myeloproliferative disorder of the bone marrow with suppressed (low) erythropoietin levels, whereas secondary polycythaemia is driven by chronic hypoxia or excess erythropoietin secretion
questions.explanation: Polycythaemia vera is an autonomous neoplastic proliferation of myeloid stem cells (elevating RBCs, WBCs, and platelets) with feedback-suppressed EPO, whereas secondary polycythaemia is a compensatory response to hypoxia or inappropriate EPO secretion.
questions.section: Erythrocyte Membrane, Gas Transport & Blood Groups

questions.text: How does erythropoietin act on the bone marrow, and how long does it take after an acute hypoxic stimulus for newly formed RBCs to appear in the circulation?
options: It causes mature RBCs to divide in blood; effect appears in $6$ hours
It stimulates CFU-E differentiation into proerythroblasts and accelerates maturation; new RBCs appear in $4$ to $5$ days
It prevents splenic destruction of old RBCs; effect appears in $1$ day
It inhibits haemoglobin synthesis; effect appears in $14$ days
questions.correctAnswer: B. It stimulates CFU-E differentiation into proerythroblasts and accelerates maturation; new RBCs appear in $4$ to $5$ days
questions.explanation: Erythropoietin stimulates the differentiation of CFU-E into proerythroblasts, accelerates haemoglobin synthesis, and speeds up maturation, with newly formed RBCs entering circulation in $4$ to $5$ days.
questions.section: Erythrocyte Membrane, Gas Transport & Blood Groups

questions.text: Chemically, what are the ABO blood group antigens (agglutinogens) on the RBC membrane, and when do ABO antigens and naturally occurring antibodies first appear?
options: Pure triglycerides; both appear at puberty
Oligosaccharides on membrane glycoproteins/glycolipids; antigens appear in the $6\text{th}$ month of fetal life, while antibodies develop $2$ to $3$ months after birth
Nucleic acid polymers; antibodies appear in utero while antigens appear after birth
Free plasma proteins; both appear only after blood transfusion
questions.correctAnswer: B. Oligosaccharides on membrane glycoproteins/glycolipids; antigens appear in the $6\text{th}$ month of fetal life, while antibodies develop $2$ to $3$ months after birth
questions.explanation: A and B agglutinogens are carbohydrate determinants on membrane glycoproteins and glycolipids that appear around the $6\text{th}$ fetal month, whereas anti-A and anti-B agglutinins develop $2$ to $3$ months postnatally.
questions.section: Erythrocyte Membrane, Gas Transport & Blood Groups

questions.text: What are the normal average circulating red blood cell counts in a healthy adult male and a healthy adult female respectively?
options: Males $3.5\ \text{million}/\text{mm}^3$; females $3.0\ \text{million}/\text{mm}^3$
Males $6.5\ \text{million}/\text{mm}^3$; females $6.0\ \text{million}/\text{mm}^3$
Males $4.5\ \text{million}/\text{mm}^3$; females $5.0\ \text{million}/\text{mm}^3$
Males $5.0\ \text{million}/\text{mm}^3$; females $4.5\ \text{million}/\text{mm}^3$
questions.correctAnswer: D. Males $5.0\ \text{million}/\text{mm}^3$; females $4.5\ \text{million}/\text{mm}^3$
questions.explanation: The normal adult RBC count averages $5.0\ \text{million}/\text{mm}^3$ ($4.5$ to $5.5\ \text{million}/\text{mm}^3$) in males and $4.5\ \text{million}/\text{mm}^3$ ($4.0$ to $5.0\ \text{million}/\text{mm}^3$) in females.
questions.section: Erythrocyte Membrane, Gas Transport & Blood Groups

questions.text: Structurally, how is the iron-containing pigment moiety (heme) of haemoglobin assembled?
options: Two benzene rings linked to a ferric ($Fe^{3+}$) ion
Six indole rings complexed with a copper atom
Four amino acid chains bound to a zinc atom
Four pyrrole rings linked by methene bridges (protoporphyrin IX) complexed with a central ferrous ($Fe^{2+}$) iron atom
questions.correctAnswer: D. Four pyrrole rings linked by methene bridges (protoporphyrin IX) complexed with a central ferrous ($Fe^{2+}$) iron atom
questions.explanation: Heme consists of a tetrapyrrole porphyrin ring (four pyrrole rings joined by methene bridges) with a central ferrous iron atom ($Fe^{2+}$) coordinated to the pyrrole nitrogens and the globin chain.
questions.section: Erythrocyte Membrane, Gas Transport & Blood Groups

questions.text: Which formula and normal adult reference range correctly define Mean Corpuscular Haemoglobin Concentration (MCHC)?
options: $\text{MCHC} = \frac{\text{PCV (%)} \times 10}{\text{RBC count}}$; normal range $78%$ to $90%$
$\text{MCHC} = \frac{\text{Hb (g/dL)} \times 10}{\text{RBC count}}$; normal range $27%$ to $32%$
$\text{MCHC} = \frac{\text{PCV (%)} \times 100}{\text{Hb (g/dL)}}$; normal range $40%$ to $45%$
$\text{MCHC} = \frac{\text{Hb (g/dL)} \times 100}{\text{PCV (%)}}$; normal range $30%$ to $38%$ (or $30$ to $38\ \text{g/dL}$)
questions.correctAnswer: D. $\text{MCHC} = \frac{\text{Hb (g/dL)} \times 100}{\text{PCV (%)}}$; normal range $30%$ to $38%$ (or $30$ to $38\ \text{g/dL}$)
questions.explanation: MCHC expresses the concentration of haemoglobin per unit volume of packed red blood cells, calculated as $\frac{\text{Hb} \times 100}{\text{PCV}}$, normally ranging from $30%$ to $38%$.

questions.text: Approximately what percentage of the dry weight of a mature human erythrocyte is composed of haemoglobin, and which organelles are absent from its cytoplasm?
options: $95%$ haemoglobin; lacks nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, and Golgi apparatus
$50%$ haemoglobin; lacks only the nucleus while retaining abundant mitochondria
$33%$ haemoglobin; retains ribosomes and rough endoplasmic reticulum
$75%$ haemoglobin; retains a Golgi apparatus for lipid secretion
questions.correctAnswer: A. $95%$ haemoglobin; lacks nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, and Golgi apparatus
questions.explanation: Haemoglobin accounts for about $95%$ of the dry weight (and $33%$ of the wet weight) of a mature RBC, which expels its nucleus and loses mitochondria, ribosomes, and Golgi apparatus during maturation.

questions.text: Why is continuous ATP supply to the membrane-bound $Na^+/K^+$-ATPase pump critical for mature red blood cell survival?
options: It prevents intracellular $Na^+$ accumulation, water influx, osmotic swelling, and cell lysis
It actively pumps $O_2$ molecules into the cell against a concentration gradient
It transports $HCO_3^-$ out of the cell during the chloride shift
It synthesizes membrane phospholipids to repair capillary tears
questions.correctAnswer: A. It prevents intracellular $Na^+$ accumulation, water influx, osmotic swelling, and cell lysis
questions.explanation: By extruding $3\ Na^+$ for every $2\ K^+$ imported, the $Na^+/K^+$-ATPase pump maintains intracellular osmotic balance, preventing water influx and osmotic lysis.

questions.text: In describing RBC colour abnormalities on a stained blood smear, what do hypochromia and polychromasia indicate respectively?
options: Hypochromia: bluish-grey tint; polychromasia: complete absence of stain
Hypochromia: deep red staining; polychromasia: loss of central pallor
Hypochromia: pale RBCs with central pallor exceeding one-third of cell diameter due to low Hb; polychromasia: bluish-grey tint indicating immature reticulocytes containing residual RNA
Hypochromia: excess iron accumulation; polychromasia: senile erythrocytes
questions.correctAnswer: C. Hypochromia: pale RBCs with central pallor exceeding one-third of cell diameter due to low Hb; polychromasia: bluish-grey tint indicating immature reticulocytes containing residual RNA
questions.explanation: Hypochromic cells appear pale with an enlarged central pallor ($> \frac{1}{3}$ of cell diameter) due to reduced haemoglobin content, whereas polychromasia reflects bluish-grey staining of young reticulocytes rich in residual RNA.

questions.text: In newborns and children up to approximately $20$ years of age, where does active red blood cell production occur?
options: Exclusively within the liver and spleen
In the red bone marrow of all bones, including the shafts of long bones
Exclusively within the sternum and skull
Within peripheral lymph nodes
questions.correctAnswer: B. In the red bone marrow of all bones, including the shafts of long bones
questions.explanation: From birth until about $20$ years of age, RBCs are actively produced in the red bone marrow of all bones, including the diaphyses (shafts) of long bones.

questions.text: What is the normal physiological fate of the globin polypeptide chains liberated during red blood cell destruction?
options: Excreted unchanged in the urine
Hydrolyzed into amino acids and returned to the body's amino acid pool for new protein synthesis
Converted directly into bilirubin in the spleen
Stored permanently as insoluble granules in the liver
questions.correctAnswer: B. Hydrolyzed into amino acids and returned to the body's amino acid pool for new protein synthesis
questions.explanation: Globin is broken down into its constituent amino acids, which enter the systemic amino acid pool to be reused for synthesizing new proteins, including new globin chains.

questions.text: From an evolutionary and physiological standpoint, why are red blood cells indispensable for sustaining aerobic metabolism in large multicellular vertebrates?
options: They actively synthesize glucose for peripheral organs
They generate the hydrostatic pressure required for arterial flow
They directly phagocytose circulating bacterial pathogens
They provide a specialized intracellular vehicle to transport large quantities of $O_2$ from the lungs to tissues
questions.correctAnswer: D. They provide a specialized intracellular vehicle to transport large quantities of $O_2$ from the lungs to tissues
questions.explanation: Because oxygen has very low solubility in plasma, red blood cells packed with haemoglobin are required to carry sufficient $O_2$ to support aerobic cellular respiration across tissues.

questions.text: During $CO_2$ uptake in systemic capillaries, bicarbonate ions ($HCO_3^-$) diffuse out of erythrocytes into the plasma. How do RBCs maintain electrical neutrality during this process?
options: By pumping $Na^+$ out of the cell
By exporting $K^+$ ions into plasma
By releasing $H^+$ ions into plasma
By importing chloride ions ($Cl^-$) from plasma into the RBC (chloride shift / Hamburger phenomenon)
questions.correctAnswer: D. By importing chloride ions ($Cl^-$) from plasma into the RBC (chloride shift / Hamburger phenomenon)
questions.explanation: As negatively charged $HCO_3^-$ exits the RBC down its concentration gradient, negatively charged $Cl^-$ enters via Band 3 protein (the chloride shift), preserving electrical neutrality.

questions.text: Why does excessive red blood cell destruction lead to haemolytic (pre-hepatic) jaundice?
options: Complete obstruction of the common bile duct prevents bile outflow
Hepatocytes lose the ability to synthesize plasma albumin
Excess iron pigments directly stain the sclera yellow
Accelerated haemoglobin breakdown generates large amounts of unconjugated bilirubin that exceed the liver's conjugating capacity
questions.correctAnswer: D. Accelerated haemoglobin breakdown generates large amounts of unconjugated bilirubin that exceed the liver's conjugating capacity
questions.explanation: In haemolytic jaundice, massive RBC destruction overwhelms hepatic glucuronidation, elevating unconjugated bilirubin in the blood and causing yellow discoloration of skin and sclerae.

questions.text: What are the approximate mean surface area and mean cellular volume of a normal mature human red blood cell?
options: Surface area $60\ \mu\text{m}^2$; volume $45\ \mu\text{m}^3$
Surface area $120\ \mu\text{m}^2$; volume $87\ \mu\text{m}^3$
Surface area $240\ \mu\text{m}^2$; volume $150\ \mu\text{m}^3$
Surface area $80\ \mu\text{m}^2$; volume $110\ \mu\text{m}^3$
questions.correctAnswer: B. Surface area $120\ \mu\text{m}^2$; volume $87\ \mu\text{m}^3$
questions.explanation: A normal human erythrocyte has an average surface area of approximately $120\ \mu\text{m}^2$ and an average volume of about $87\ \mu\text{m}^3$ ($78$ to $90\ \mu\text{m}^3$).

questions.text: How does glucose enter the mature human red blood cell from the surrounding plasma?
options: Active sodium-glucose cotransport requiring ATP
Strictly insulin-dependent vesicular endocytosis
Simple diffusion through cholesterol channels
Insulin-independent facilitated diffusion via GLUT1 transporters
questions.correctAnswer: D. Insulin-independent facilitated diffusion via GLUT1 transporters
questions.explanation: Mature erythrocytes lack insulin receptors and take up glucose continuously via insulin-independent facilitated diffusion mediated by GLUT1 membrane transporters.

questions.text: What is the general medical term for a pathological reduction in the circulating red blood cell count, haemoglobin concentration, or packed cell volume below normal reference limits for age and sex?
options: Erythrocytosis
Polycythaemia
Anaemia
Reticulocytosis
questions.correctAnswer: C. Anaemia
questions.explanation: Anaemia is defined as a pathological decrease in RBC count, haemoglobin concentration, and/or haematocrit below normal reference values, reducing the oxygen-carrying capacity of blood.

questions.text: What is the normal circulating reticulocyte count in a healthy adult, and how many total days are required for a proerythroblast to mature into a biconcave erythrocyte?
options: $5%$ to $10%$; $21$ days total
$\le 1%$; $7$ days total ($5$ days to reticulocyte plus $2$ days to mature RBC)
$2%$ to $6%$; $14$ days total
$0%$; $3$ days total
questions.correctAnswer: B. $\le 1%$; $7$ days total ($5$ days to reticulocyte plus $2$ days to mature RBC)
questions.explanation: Reticulocytes normally represent $\le 1%$ of adult circulating RBCs (showing organelle remnants on supravital staining). Erythropoiesis takes $7$ days total: $5$ days to reach the reticulocyte stage and $2$ more days to mature into an erythrocyte.

questions.text: How does extravascular haemolysis differ fundamentally from intravascular haemolysis?
options: Extravascular haemolysis occurs inside arterial capillaries; intravascular occurs in the bone marrow

Extravascular haemolysis involves macrophage phagocytosis within the reticuloendothelial system (spleen/liver), whereas intravascular haemolysis involves direct RBC rupture within the bloodstream releasing free haemoglobin
Extravascular haemolysis releases free haemoglobin directly into urine; intravascular produces only bilirubin
Extravascular haemolysis occurs only in neonates; intravascular is the normal adult pathway
questions.correctAnswer: B. Extravascular haemolysis involves macrophage phagocytosis within the reticuloendothelial system (spleen/liver), whereas intravascular haemolysis involves direct RBC rupture within the bloodstream releasing free haemoglobin
questions.explanation: Normal senile RBC clearance is extravascular (within splenic/hepatic macrophages), whereas intravascular haemolysis releases free haemoglobin directly into plasma, where it is bound by haptoglobin.

questions.text: What is the fundamental molecular defect characterizing the thalassaemias ($\alpha$-thalassaemia and $\beta$-thalassaemia)?
options: A qualitative amino acid substitution that causes haemoglobin polymerization
An acquired autoimmune antibody directed against RBC Band 3 protein
A deficiency of dietary folic acid impairing nuclear division

A quantitative reduction or complete absence in the synthesis of normal $\alpha$- or $\beta$-globin polypeptide chains, leading to imbalanced chain ratios, ineffective erythropoiesis, and microcytic hypochromic anaemia
questions.correctAnswer: D. A quantitative reduction or complete absence in the synthesis of normal $\alpha$- or $\beta$-globin polypeptide chains, leading to imbalanced chain ratios, ineffective erythropoiesis, and microcytic hypochromic anaemia
questions.explanation: Unlike sickle cell disease (a qualitative structural defect), thalassaemias are quantitative disorders of reduced or absent $\alpha$- or $\beta$-globin chain production; excess unpaired chains precipitate and damage erythroid cells.

questions.text: Which combination accurately pairs supportive trace metals and hemopoietic growth factors with their roles in erythropoiesis?
options: Calcium synthesizes globin; IL-$1$ inhibits stem cells
Sodium forms heme; IL-$2$ lyses normoblasts
Zinc replaces iron in heme; IL-$8$ extrudes the nucleus
Copper aids intestinal iron absorption, cobalt/nickel aid iron utilization, and IL-$3$, IL-$6$, and IL-$11$ stimulate stem cell proliferation
questions.correctAnswer: D. Copper aids intestinal iron absorption, cobalt/nickel aid iron utilization, and IL-$3$, IL-$6$, and IL-$11$ stimulate stem cell proliferation
questions.explanation: Beyond iron (for heme), copper is essential for iron absorption, cobalt and nickel assist iron utilization, and interleukins (IL-$3$, IL-$6$, and osteoblast-derived IL-$11$) stimulate pluripotent stem cell proliferation.

questions.text: What is the antigenic and antibody basis for classifying Blood Group O as the universal donor and Blood Group AB as the universal recipient in the ABO system?
options: Group O plasma lacks antibodies; Group AB RBCs lack antigens
Group O RBCs have both A and B antigens; Group AB plasma has both anti-A and anti-B
Group O RBCs are resistant to complement lysis; Group AB RBCs have no membrane proteins
Group O RBCs lack A and B agglutinogens; Group AB plasma lacks anti-A and anti-B agglutinins
questions.correctAnswer: D. Group O RBCs lack A and B agglutinogens; Group AB plasma lacks anti-A and anti-B agglutinins
questions.explanation: Group O RBCs have no A or B surface antigens to be attacked by recipient antibodies, while Group AB plasma lacks anti-A and anti-B antibodies to attack donor RBCs.

questions.text: Which physiological property allows red blood cells to remain uniformly dispersed throughout circulating plasma without settling during normal blood flow?
options: Suspension stability
Capillary margination
Osmotic fragility
Diapedesis
questions.correctAnswer: A. Suspension stability
questions.explanation: Suspension stability refers to the ability of RBCs to remain uniformly suspended in circulating blood; loss of suspension stability increases the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR).

questions.text: Why is the binding of oxygen to haemoglobin classified as oxygenation rather than oxidation, and how many $O_2$ molecules bind to one fully saturated haemoglobin molecule?
options: Iron transitions from $Fe^{2+}$ to $Fe^{3+}$; binds $2\ O_2$ molecules
Oxygen forms a permanent covalent bond with globin; binds $1\ O_2$ molecule
Oxygen binds loosely and reversibly while iron remains in the ferrous ($Fe^{2+}$) state; binds $4\ O_2$ molecules
Oxygen displaces the porphyrin ring; binds $8\ O_2$ molecules
questions.correctAnswer: C. Oxygen binds loosely and reversibly while iron remains in the ferrous ($Fe^{2+}$) state; binds $4\ O_2$ molecules
questions.explanation: Oxygenation is a loose, reversible association in which each of the four heme $Fe^{2+}$ atoms binds one $O_2$ molecule ($4\ O_2$ per Hb, or $1.34\ \text{mL}\ O_2/\text{g}$ Hb) without oxidizing $Fe^{2+}$ to $Fe^{3+}$.

questions.text: How are red blood cells classified when their MCV is below $78\ \text{fL}$ and their MCHC is below $30%$?
options: Macrocytic and normochromic
Normocytic and normochromic
Microcytic and hypochromic
Macrocytic and hypochromic
questions.correctAnswer: C. Microcytic and hypochromic
questions.explanation: An MCV below the normal range indicates small cells (microcytic), and an MCHC below $30%$ indicates reduced haemoglobin concentration (hypochromic).

questions.text: At which earliest recognizable nucleated stage of erythropoiesis does the biochemical synthesis of haemoglobin begin, even though it is not yet microscopically visible?
options: Early normoblast
Proerythroblast
Intermediate normoblast
Late normoblast
questions.correctAnswer: B. Proerythroblast
questions.explanation: Haemoglobin synthesis commences at the proerythroblast stage, although it only becomes visible microscopically at the intermediate normoblast stage.

questions.text: Why do mature human red blood cells inevitably age and have a strictly finite lifespan of about $120$ days?
options: They exhaust their chromosomal telomeres during peripheral mitosis
Lacking a nucleus and ribosomes, they cannot synthesize new enzymes or membrane proteins, leading to progressive metabolic decline and membrane rigidity
Plasma antibodies progressively lyse all RBCs after $4$ months
Haemoglobin crystallizes spontaneously after $100$ pulmonary transits
questions.correctAnswer: B. Lacking a nucleus and ribosomes, they cannot synthesize new enzymes or membrane proteins, leading to progressive metabolic decline and membrane rigidity
questions.explanation: Because mature RBCs lack nuclei and ribosomes, they cannot replace worn-out glycolytic enzymes or membrane proteins; as ATP production falls, membranes become fragile and rigid.

questions.text: What is the fundamental cellular mechanism by which Vitamin $B_{12}$ or folic acid deficiency produces megaloblastic anaemia?
options: Direct oxidation of ferrous iron to ferric iron inside mature RBCs
Destruction of spectrin filaments in the erythrocyte cytoskeleton
Excess production of erythropoietin by the renal tubules
Impaired DNA synthesis slows nuclear maturation and cell division while cytoplasmic RNA/haemoglobin synthesis continues, producing abnormally large, fragile macrocytes
questions.correctAnswer: D. Impaired DNA synthesis slows nuclear maturation and cell division while cytoplasmic RNA/haemoglobin synthesis continues, producing abnormally large, fragile macrocytes
questions.explanation: Deficiency of Vitamin $B_{12}$ or folate impairs thymidine/DNA synthesis, creating nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony that results in large nucleated megaloblasts in marrow and oversized macrocytes in blood.

questions.text: Which specific cells secrete approximately $85%$ to $90%$ of circulating erythropoietin in response to hypoxia?
options: Juxtaglomerular smooth muscle cells of the afferent arteriole
Hepatocytes of the liver lobules
Gastric parietal cells
Peritubular capillary endothelial/interstitial cells of the kidney
questions.correctAnswer: D. Peritubular capillary endothelial/interstitial cells of the kidney
questions.explanation: The vast majority ($85%$ to $90%$) of erythropoietin (a $165$-amino-acid glycoprotein) is secreted by peritubular capillary endothelial/interstitial cells in the kidney, with minor secretion by the liver and brain.

questions.text: Inside hepatocytes, unconjugated bilirubin is made water-soluble for biliary excretion by conjugation with which substance, and what does colonic bacterial action convert it into?
options: Conjugated with glycine; converted into transferrin
Conjugated with sulfuric acid; converted into biliverdin
Conjugated with hydrochloric acid; converted into haemosiderin
Conjugated with glucuronic acid; converted into urobilinogen and excreted mainly in faeces as stercobilin
questions.correctAnswer: D. Conjugated with glucuronic acid; converted into urobilinogen and excreted mainly in faeces as stercobilin
questions.explanation: Hepatocytes conjugate bilirubin with glucuronic acid (via UDP-glucuronyl transferase); in the intestine, bacteria convert it into urobilinogen, most of which is excreted as stercobilin (giving stool its brown colour), with a small fraction excreted in urine as urobilin.

questions.text: Although mature erythrocytes in almost all mammals are non-nucleated, which mammal represents a classic exception by retaining nucleated red blood cells in its mature circulation?
options: Elephant
Camel
Whale
Giraffe
questions.correctAnswer: B. Camel
questions.explanation: The camel is a notable mammalian exception that possesses oval, nucleated red blood cells in its mature peripheral circulation.

questions.text: What is the normal blood haemoglobin concentration range in healthy adult males and healthy adult females respectively?
options: Males $10$ to $12\ \text{g/dL}$; females $8$ to $10\ \text{g/dL}$
Males $18$ to $22\ \text{g/dL}$; females $16$ to $18\ \text{g/dL}$
Males $14$ to $16\ \text{g/dL}$; females $12$ to $14\ \text{g/dL}$
Males $12$ to $13\ \text{g/dL}$; females $12$ to $13\ \text{g/dL}$
questions.correctAnswer: C. Males $14$ to $16\ \text{g/dL}$; females $12$ to $14\ \text{g/dL}$
questions.explanation: Normal adult haemoglobin concentration is $14$ to $16\ \text{g/dL}$ (average $15\ \text{g/dL}$) in males and $12$ to $14\ \text{g/dL}$ in females.

questions.text: Which formula and normal adult reference range correctly define Mean Corpuscular Haemoglobin (MCH)?
options: $\text{MCH} = \frac{\text{PCV (%)} \times 10}{\text{RBC count}}$; normal range $78$ to $90\ \text{pg}$
$\text{MCH} = \frac{\text{Hb (g/dL)} \times 100}{\text{PCV (%)}}$; normal range $30$ to $38\ \text{pg}$
$\text{MCH} = \frac{\text{Hb (g/dL)} \times 10}{\text{RBC count (millions/mm}^3\text{)}}$; normal range $27$ to $32\ \text{pg}$
$\text{MCH} = \frac{\text{Hb (%)}}{\text{RBC (%)}}$; normal range $0.8$ to $1.2\ \text{pg}$
questions.correctAnswer: C. $\text{MCH} = \frac{\text{Hb (g/dL)} \times 10}{\text{RBC count (millions/mm}^3\text{)}}$; normal range $27$ to $32\ \text{pg}$
questions.explanation: MCH represents the average weight of haemoglobin in a single RBC, calculated as $\frac{\text{Hb} \times 10}{\text{RBC count}}$, with a normal value of $27$ to $32\ \text{pg}$.

questions.text: Which major integral transmembrane protein of the erythrocyte membrane serves both as an anchor point for ankyrin and as the anion exchanger mediating $Cl^-/HCO_3^-$ exchange?
options: Glycophorin A
Band 3 protein
Tropomodulin
Adducin
questions.correctAnswer: B. Band 3 protein
questions.explanation: Band 3 protein (anion exchanger 1) is the most abundant integral membrane protein in RBCs; it anchors the spectrin-actin cytoskeleton via ankyrin and mediates the 1:1 chloride-bicarbonate shift.

questions.text: Small quantities of haemoglobin spontaneously oxidize to non-functional methemoglobin ($Fe^{3+}$) daily. Which intracellular RBC enzyme system performs $95%$ of the reduction back to ferrous haemoglobin ($Fe^{2+}$)?
options: Carbonic anhydrase II
NADH-dependent methemoglobin reductase (Diaphorase I)
Superoxide dismutase
Ferrochelatase
questions.correctAnswer: B. NADH-dependent methemoglobin reductase (Diaphorase I)
questions.explanation: The NADH-dependent methemoglobin reductase system (Diaphorase I) accounts for roughly $95%$ of intracellular methemoglobin reduction back to functional $Fe^{2+}$ haemoglobin.

questions.text: Which of the following correctly matches an abnormal RBC shape (poikilocyte) with its classic morphological appearance?
options: Spherocyte: small, dense, spherical RBC lacking central pallor; Target cell (codocyte): bull's-eye appearance with central haemoglobin dot; Drepanocyte: crescent/sickle shape
Spherocyte: elongated cigar shape; Target cell: spiked projections; Drepanocyte: teardrop shape
Spherocyte: expanded central pallor; Target cell: biconcave normal disc; Drepanocyte: spherical shape
Spherocyte: ring-shaped hollow cell; Target cell: crescent shape; Drepanocyte: fragmented helmet shape
questions.correctAnswer: A. Spherocyte: small, dense, spherical RBC lacking central pallor; Target cell (codocyte): bull's-eye appearance with central haemoglobin dot; Drepanocyte: crescent/sickle shape
questions.explanation: Spherocytes lose biconcavity and central pallor; target cells (codocytes) show a central haemoglobin density surrounded by a pale ring; drepanocytes are crescent-shaped sickle cells.

questions.text: When does the myeloid stage of erythropoiesis—in which red bone marrow takes over RBC production—begin during human development?
options: During the first $4$ weeks of gestation
During the second month of gestation
Immediately after puberty
During the last $3$ months of intrauterine life
questions.correctAnswer: D. During the last $3$ months of intrauterine life
questions.explanation: The myeloid stage begins during the last $3$ months of intrauterine life, as red bone marrow progressively replaces the liver as the main site of erythropoiesis.

questions.text: Inside reticuloendothelial macrophages following senile RBC destruction, haemoglobin is initially broken down into which three primary components?
options: Bilirubin, albumin, and glucose
Ferritin, transferrin, and urobilin
Amino acids, fatty acids, and glycerol
Iron, globin, and porphyrin
questions.correctAnswer: D. Iron, globin, and porphyrin
questions.explanation: Tissue macrophages cleave haemoglobin into its three structural constituents: iron, the globin protein chains, and the porphyrin ring.

questions.text: In a healthy adult, red blood cells normally occupy approximately what percentage of total whole blood volume (the haematocrit)?
questions.explanation: Whole blood consists of roughly $55%$ liquid plasma and $40%$ to $45%$ packed red blood cells, with leukocytes and platelets occupying less than $1%$.

questions.text: How do red blood cells contribute significantly to systemic acid-base balance in the blood?
options: By excreting hydrogen ions directly through the alveolar membrane
By synthesizing ammonia from plasma urea
Through the buffering action of haemoglobin, which provides roughly six times the buffering power of plasma proteins
By actively secreting hydrochloric acid into venous plasma
questions.correctAnswer: C. Through the buffering action of haemoglobin, which provides roughly six times the buffering power of plasma proteins
questions.explanation: Haemoglobin is a major blood buffer (about $6$ times more potent than plasma proteins); deoxygenated haemoglobin has a higher $pK$, allowing its histidine residues to bind $H^+$ generated from carbonic acid dissociation.

questions.text: What is the primary pathophysiological sequence during an acute ABO-incompatible haemolytic transfusion reaction?
options: Recipient antibodies bind donor RBC antigens, causing agglutination, complement-mediated intravascular haemolysis, haemoglobinaemia, and haemoglobinuria
Donor RBCs immediately differentiate into leukocytes in recipient marrow
Recipient plasma proteins induce harmless rouleaux formation that resolves spontaneously
Donor platelets prevent oxygen release from recipient haemoglobin
questions.correctAnswer: A. Recipient antibodies bind donor RBC antigens, causing agglutination, complement-mediated intravascular haemolysis, haemoglobinaemia, and haemoglobinuria
questions.explanation: In an incompatible transfusion, pre-formed recipient antibodies agglutinate donor RBCs and activate complement, causing rapid intravascular haemolysis and release of free haemoglobin into plasma and urine.

questions.text: Which set of morphometric dimensions accurately describes a normal mature human biconcave erythrocyte?
options: Diameter $10.0\ \mu\text{m}$; central thickness $2.5\ \mu\text{m}$; peripheral thickness $1.0\ \mu\text{m}$
Diameter $5.5\ \mu\text{m}$; central thickness $1.5\ \mu\text{m}$; peripheral thickness $3.0\ \mu\text{m}$
Diameter $8.5\ \mu\text{m}$; central thickness $2.2\ \mu\text{m}$; peripheral thickness $1.0\ \mu\text{m}$
Diameter $7.2\ \mu\text{m}$; central thickness $1.0\ \mu\text{m}$; peripheral thickness $2.2\ \mu\text{m}$
questions.correctAnswer: D. Diameter $7.2\ \mu\text{m}$; central thickness $1.0\ \mu\text{m}$; peripheral thickness $2.2\ \mu\text{m}$
questions.explanation: A normal mature erythrocyte has a mean diameter of $7.2\ \mu\text{m}$ (range $6.9$ to $7.4\ \mu\text{m}$), a central thickness of $1.0\ \mu\text{m}$, and a peripheral thickness of $2.2\ \mu\text{m}$.

questions.text: Because mature human erythrocytes lack mitochondria, through which metabolic pathway do they generate their ATP, and what is its final end product?
options: Citric acid cycle; carbon dioxide and water
Anaerobic glycolysis (Embden-Meyerhof pathway); lactate
Beta-oxidation of fatty acids; acetyl-CoA
Oxidative phosphorylation; pyruvate
questions.correctAnswer: B. Anaerobic glycolysis (Embden-Meyerhof pathway); lactate
questions.explanation: Without mitochondria, mature RBCs depend exclusively on anaerobic glycolysis (Embden-Meyerhof pathway) for ATP production, reducing pyruvate to lactate to regenerate $NAD^+$.

questions.text: What is the general medical term for a pathological increase in the circulating red blood cell count above normal physiological limits?
options: Polycythaemia
Anaemia
Leukocytosis
Thrombocytosis
questions.correctAnswer: A. Polycythaemia
questions.explanation: Polycythaemia refers to a pathological elevation in the RBC count (typically above $7\ \text{million}/\text{mm}^3$), which increases blood viscosity and haematocrit.

questions.text: Which developmental events occur at the late normoblast (orthochromic erythroblast) stage of erythropoiesis?
options: Onset of rapid mitotic division and nucleolar enlargement
Initial transcription of globin mRNA
Cessation of mitosis, shrinkage into an ink-spot nucleus, and nuclear extrusion by pyknosis
Complete dissolution of all haemoglobin into biliverdin
questions.correctAnswer: C. Cessation of mitosis, shrinkage into an ink-spot nucleus, and nuclear extrusion by pyknosis
questions.explanation: In the late normoblast ($8$ to $10\ \mu\text{m}$), active mitosis ceases, the cytoplasm becomes acidophilic, and the nucleus condenses into a dense "ink-spot" nucleus that is extruded to form a reticulocyte.

questions.text: What anatomical feature of the spleen specifically triggers the mechanical destruction of aged, fragile red blood cells?
options: Strongly acidic pH within the splenic white pulp
High concentrations of bile salts in the splenic vein
Very narrow capillaries and endothelial slits in the splenic red pulp that rigid senile RBCs cannot squeeze through without rupturing
Hypotonic plasma environment within the splenic artery
questions.correctAnswer: C. Very narrow capillaries and endothelial slits in the splenic red pulp that rigid senile RBCs cannot squeeze through without rupturing
questions.explanation: As RBCs age, they lose membrane deformability; when forced through the extremely narrow capillaries and slits of the splenic red pulp, senile RBCs fragment and are phagocytosed by macrophages.

questions.text: Under conditions of low oxygen tension, how does Haemoglobin S (HbS) cause the characteristic pathology of Sickle Cell Disease?
options: Deoxygenated HbS polymerizes into rigid, elongated tactoids/fibres that deform RBCs into fragile crescent (sickle) shapes, causing microvascular occlusion and chronic haemolysis
Oxygenated HbS binds irreversibly to plasma albumin and blocks renal tubules
HbS converts into methemoglobin and prevents carbonic anhydrase activity
HbS causes RBCs to swell into giant macrocytes that cannot exit the bone marrow
questions.correctAnswer: A. Deoxygenated HbS polymerizes into rigid, elongated tactoids/fibres that deform RBCs into fragile crescent (sickle) shapes, causing microvascular occlusion and chronic haemolysis
questions.explanation: When deoxygenated, hydrophobic valine residues on HbS promote polymerization into rigid intracellular fibres, distorting the RBC into a sickle shape that obstructs microvessels and undergoes premature haemolysis.

questions.text: Vitamin $B_{12}$ and folic acid are essential maturation factors for erythropoiesis. What is their primary biochemical role, and which gastric cells secrete the intrinsic factor needed for Vitamin $B_{12}$ absorption?
options: Heme iron chelation; chief cells
Spectrin cross-linking; enterochromaffin cells
DNA synthesis for nuclear maturation and cell division; parietal (oxyntic) cells
Glycolytic ATP production; mucous neck cells
questions.correctAnswer: C. DNA synthesis for nuclear maturation and cell division; parietal (oxyntic) cells
questions.explanation: Vitamin $B_{12}$ and folic acid are essential for nucleic acid (DNA) synthesis during erythroid maturation. Gastric parietal cells secrete intrinsic factor, which is required for Vitamin $B_{12}$ absorption in the terminal ileum.

questions.text: To which immunoglobulin classes do naturally occurring ABO agglutinins (anti-A, anti-B) and immune Rh antibodies (anti-D) predominantly belong respectively?
options: ABO are IgG (cross placenta); anti-D are IgM (cannot cross placenta)
Both ABO and anti-D are strictly IgA
ABO are predominantly IgM (large pentamers, cannot cross placenta); anti-D are predominantly IgG (monomers, can cross placenta)
ABO are IgE; anti-D are IgD
questions.correctAnswer: C. ABO are predominantly IgM (large pentamers, cannot cross placenta); anti-D are predominantly IgG (monomers, can cross placenta)
questions.explanation: Naturally occurring anti-A and anti-B are predominantly large pentameric IgM antibodies that do not cross the placenta, whereas anti-D antibodies are smaller IgG molecules capable of crossing the placental barrier.

questions.text: When anticoagulated blood stands in a vertical tube, red blood cells tend to stack together like a pile of coins (rouleaux formation). Which plasma proteins primarily accelerate this phenomenon?
options: Albumin and transferrin
Prothrombin and plasminogen
Fibrinogen and globulins
Haptoglobin and ceruloplasmin
questions.correctAnswer: C. Fibrinogen and globulins
questions.explanation: High-molecular-weight plasma proteins—specifically fibrinogen and globulins—reduce the electrostatic repulsion between RBCs and accelerate rouleaux formation.

questions.text: How does fetal haemoglobin (HbF) differ structurally and functionally from normal adult haemoglobin (HbA)?
options: HbF has two $\alpha$- and two $\delta$-chains and a lower oxygen affinity than HbA
HbF has two $\alpha$- and two $\gamma$-chains and a higher oxygen affinity than HbA due to weaker $2,3$-DPG binding
HbF has four $\gamma$-chains and transports only carbon dioxide
HbF contains ferric iron ($Fe^{3+}$) and shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the right
questions.correctAnswer: B. HbF has two $\alpha$- and two $\gamma$-chains and a higher oxygen affinity than HbA due to weaker $2,3$-DPG binding
questions.explanation: HbF ($\alpha_2\gamma_2$) replaces $\beta$-chains with $\gamma$-chains, which bind $2,3$-DPG less avidly; this gives HbF a higher affinity for $O_2$, facilitating placental oxygen transfer from mother to fetus.

questions.text: For a blood sample with $\text{PCV} = 45%$, $\text{RBC count} = 5.0\ \text{million}/\text{mm}^3$, and $\text{Hb} = 15\ \text{g/dL}$, what are the calculated values of MCV, MCH, and MCHC respectively?
options: $\text{MCV} = 90\ \text{fL}$; $\text{MCH} = 30\ \text{pg}$; $\text{MCHC} = 33.3%$
$\text{MCV} = 75\ \text{fL}$; $\text{MCH} = 25\ \text{pg}$; $\text{MCHC} = 30.0%$
$\text{MCV} = 90\ \text{fL}$; $\text{MCH} = 33.3\ \text{pg}$; $\text{MCHC} = 30.0%$
$\text{MCV} = 100\ \text{fL}$; $\text{MCH} = 30\ \text{pg}$; $\text{MCHC} = 35.0%$
questions.correctAnswer: A. $\text{MCV} = 90\ \text{fL}$; $\text{MCH} = 30\ \text{pg}$; $\text{MCHC} = 33.3%$
questions.explanation: $\text{MCV} = \frac{45 \times 10}{5.0} = 90\ \text{fL}$; $\text{MCH} = \frac{15 \times 10}{5.0} = 30\ \text{pg}$; $\text{MCHC} = \frac{15 \times 100}{45} = 33.3%$.

questions.text: As a developing erythroid cell matures from a proerythroblast into a mature erythrocyte, which of the following changes does NOT normally occur?
options: Progressive decrease in overall cell diameter
Condensation and eventual extrusion of the nucleus
Shift in cytoplasmic staining from acidophilic to strongly basophilic
Progressive accumulation of intracellular haemoglobin
questions.correctAnswer: C. Shift in cytoplasmic staining from acidophilic to strongly basophilic
questions.explanation: Cytoplasmic staining shifts in the opposite direction—from strongly basophilic (rich in RNA/ribosomes) in early precursors to acidophilic (eosinophilic) as haemoglobin accumulates and RNA disappears.

questions.text: Which laboratory technique is standardly used to determine the in vivo lifespan of human red blood cells?
options: Westergren sedimentation tube measurement
Supravital staining with brilliant cresyl blue
Serial hypotonic saline dilution testing
Radioisotope tagging of RBCs with radioactive chromium ($^{51}Cr$) or radioactive iron
questions.correctAnswer: D. Radioisotope tagging of RBCs with radioactive chromium ($^{51}Cr$) or radioactive iron
questions.explanation: The lifespan of RBCs is measured by tagging erythrocytes with radioisotopes such as $^{51}Cr$ and tracking the progressive decline of circulating radioactivity over time.

questions.text: In the morphological classification of anaemia, which pairing correctly matches the morphological type with a classic aetiological example?
options: Microcytic hypochromic: iron deficiency anaemia; Macrocytic normochromic: Vitamin $B_{12}$/folate deficiency; Normocytic normochromic: acute blood loss or aplastic anaemia
Microcytic hypochromic: Vitamin $B_{12}$ deficiency; Macrocytic normochromic: iron deficiency anaemia; Normocytic normochromic: thalassaemia
Microcytic hypochromic: acute haemorrhage; Macrocytic normochromic: hereditary spherocytosis; Normocytic normochromic: folic acid deficiency
Microcytic hypochromic: aplastic anaemia; Macrocytic normochromic: iron deficiency; Normocytic normochromic: megaloblastic anaemia
questions.correctAnswer: A. Microcytic hypochromic: iron deficiency anaemia; Macrocytic normochromic: Vitamin $B_{12}$/folate deficiency; Normocytic normochromic: acute blood loss or aplastic anaemia
questions.explanation: Impaired haemoglobin synthesis (iron deficiency, thalassaemia) yields microcytic hypochromic RBCs; impaired DNA synthesis ($B_{12}$/folate deficiency) yields macrocytic RBCs; acute haemorrhage or marrow aplasia yields normocytic normochromic RBCs.

questions.text: What is the single most potent physiological stimulus that accelerates the rate of erythropoiesis?
options: Hypercapnia
Hyperglycaemia
Tissue hypoxia
Metabolic alkalosis
questions.correctAnswer: C. Tissue hypoxia
questions.explanation: Tissue hypoxia (reduced oxygen delivery to tissues) is the primary physiological stimulus that triggers erythropoietin secretion and increases red blood cell production.

questions.text: What is the sequential metabolic fate of the iron-free porphyrin ring released during haemoglobin breakdown?
options: Converted directly into stercobilin inside the spleen
Reused intact to synthesize new red blood cell membranes
Degraded to biliverdin and then unconjugated bilirubin, which travels in plasma bound to albumin to the liver
Excreted directly through the lungs as volatile gases
questions.correctAnswer: C. Degraded to biliverdin and then unconjugated bilirubin, which travels in plasma bound to albumin to the liver
questions.explanation: The porphyrin ring is opened to form green biliverdin, reduced to yellow unconjugated (water-insoluble) bilirubin, and transported in plasma bound to albumin to the liver.

questions.text: Which pair of fundamental biological characteristics strictly distinguishes mature human red blood cells from white blood cells (leukocytes)?
options: Absence of a nucleus and presence of intracellular haemoglobin
Presence of mitochondria and ability to undergo mitosis in blood
Larger cellular diameter and absence of a plasma membrane
Presence of a multi-lobed nucleus and synthesis of antibodies
questions.correctAnswer: A. Absence of a nucleus and presence of intracellular haemoglobin
questions.explanation: Unlike leukocytes, which are nucleated and lack haemoglobin, mature human RBCs are anucleate and filled with haemoglobin, giving blood its red colour.

questions.text: How do red blood cells influence haemodynamics and peripheral vascular resistance within the circulatory system?
options: By contributing substantially to blood viscosity, which helps maintain peripheral resistance and arterial blood pressure
By secreting nitric oxide synthase from their nuclei to constrict arterioles
By directly contracting to propel blood through venous valves
By lowering blood density below that of water
questions.correctAnswer: A. By contributing substantially to blood viscosity, which helps maintain peripheral resistance and arterial blood pressure
questions.explanation: Because RBCs are a major determinant of blood viscosity, their concentration directly influences peripheral vascular resistance and overall haemodynamics.

questions.text: Which formula and normal adult reference range correctly define Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV)?
options: $\text{MCV} = \frac{\text{PCV (%)} \times 10}{\text{RBC count (millions/mm}^3\text{)}}$; normal range $78$ to $90\ \text{fL}$
$\text{MCV} = \frac{\text{Hb (g/dL)} \times 10}{\text{RBC count (millions/mm}^3\text{)}}$; normal range $27$ to $32\ \text{fL}$
$\text{MCV} = \frac{\text{Hb (g/dL)} \times 100}{\text{PCV (%)}}$; normal range $30$ to $38\ \text{fL}$
$\text{MCV} = \frac{\text{RBC count} \times 10}{\text{PCV (%)}}$; normal range $40$ to $45\ \text{fL}$
questions.correctAnswer: A. $\text{MCV} = \frac{\text{PCV (%)} \times 10}{\text{RBC count (millions/mm}^3\text{)}}$; normal range $78$ to $90\ \text{fL}$
questions.explanation: MCV measures the average volume of a single RBC in femtolitres ($\text{fL}$ or $\mu\text{m}^3$), calculated as $\frac{\text{PCV} \times 10}{\text{RBC count}}$, with a normal range of $78$ to $90\ \text{fL}$.

questions.text: Which pair of submembranous cytoskeletal proteins forms a flexible meshwork anchored to transmembrane proteins via ankyrin to maintain the biconcave shape of the RBC?
options: Myosin and troponin
Tubulin and dynein
Spectrin and actin
Keratin and vimentin
questions.correctAnswer: C. Spectrin and actin
questions.explanation: The erythrocyte cytoskeleton consists primarily of spectrin and actin filaments, linked via ankyrin and Band 4.1 proteins to integral membrane proteins to preserve biconcavity and flexibility.

questions.text: What is the physiological function of the Rapoport-Luebering shunt within red blood cell glycolysis?
options: Converting lactate back into glucose
Synthesizing porphyrin rings for heme assembly
Producing $2,3$-diphosphoglycerate ($2,3$-DPG) to regulate oxygen unloading from haemoglobin
Generating NADH for methemoglobin reduction
questions.correctAnswer: C. Producing $2,3$-diphosphoglycerate ($2,3$-DPG) to regulate oxygen unloading from haemoglobin
questions.explanation: The Rapoport-Luebering shunt diverts $1,3$-bisphosphoglycerate to form $2,3$-DPG, an organic phosphate that stabilizes deoxyhaemoglobin and promotes oxygen release to tissues.

questions.text: How are microcytes and macrocytes quantitatively defined based on erythrocyte diameter and MCV?
options: Microcytes $> 8\ \mu\text{m}$ ($\text{MCV} > 95\ \text{fL}$); macrocytes $< 6\ \mu\text{m}$ ($\text{MCV} < 78\ \text{fL}$)
Microcytes $7.2\ \mu\text{m}$; macrocytes $7.4\ \mu\text{m}$
Microcytes have no central pallor; macrocytes have no haemoglobin
Microcytes are abnormally small RBCs ($< 6\ \mu\text{m}$, $\text{MCV} < 78\ \text{fL}$); macrocytes are abnormally large RBCs ($> 8\ \mu\text{m}$, $\text{MCV} > 95\ \text{fL}$)
questions.correctAnswer: D. Microcytes are abnormally small RBCs ($< 6\ \mu\text{m}$, $\text{MCV} < 78\ \text{fL}$); macrocytes are abnormally large RBCs ($> 8\ \mu\text{m}$, $\text{MCV} > 95\ \text{fL}$)
questions.explanation: Microcytes are smaller than normal ($< 6\ \mu\text{m}$ diameter, low MCV), typical of iron deficiency and thalassaemia; macrocytes are larger than normal ($> 8\ \mu\text{m}$ diameter, high MCV), typical of megaloblastic anaemia.

questions.text: Starting from the third month of intrauterine life, which organ becomes the primary site of erythropoiesis during the hepatic stage?
options: Kidney
Thymus
Liver (assisted by spleen and lymphoid organs)
Pancreas
questions.correctAnswer: C. Liver (assisted by spleen and lymphoid organs)
questions.explanation: During the hepatic stage (from the $3\text{rd}$ month of fetal life), the liver assumes the primary role in RBC production, assisted by the spleen and lymphoid tissues.

questions.text: What morphological change occurs when normal human red blood cells are placed in a hypertonic ($2.0%$) sodium chloride solution?
options: Endosmosis, spherical swelling, and immediate haemolysis
No change in cell volume or shape
Exosmosis (water loss), cellular shrinkage, and spiky wrinkling (crenation)
Spontaneous rouleaux formation followed by nuclear regeneration
questions.correctAnswer: C. Exosmosis (water loss), cellular shrinkage, and spiky wrinkling (crenation)
questions.explanation: In a hypertonic solution, water leaves the erythrocyte down its osmotic gradient (exosmosis), causing shrinkage and a characteristic spiky appearance termed crenation rather than haemolysis.
